title: God does not show off like the newly rich
source_text: Εἰ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὰ καταγελαστότατα τοῦ Κέλσου θέλεις ἡμᾶς ἀπαντᾶν, ἄκουε αὐτοῦ λέγοντος· ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀγνοούμενος ὁ θεὸς ἐν ἀνθρώποις καὶ παρὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἔλαττον ἔχειν δοκῶν ἐθέλοι ἂν γνωσθῆναι καὶ τοὺς πιστεύοντάς τε καὶ ἀπιστοῦντας διαπειράσαι, καθάπερ οἱ νεόπλουτοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδεικτιῶντες; πολλὴν (γοῦν) τινα καὶ πάνυ θνητὴν φιλοτιμίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καταμαρτυροῦσι. φαμὲν οὖν ὅτι ἀγνοούμενος θεὸς ὑπὸ φαύλων ἀνθρώπων οὐ παρὰ τὸ αὐτὸς ἔλαττον ἔχειν δοκεῖν θέλοι ἂν γνωσθῆναι, ἀλλὰ τὸ τὴν γνῶσιν αὐτοῦ κακοδαιμονίας ἀπαλλάσσειν τὸν γινώσκοντα. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ διαπειράσαι θέλων τοὺς πιστεύοντας ἢ τοὺς ἀπιστοῦντας ἤτοι αὐτὸς ἀῤῥήτῳ καὶ θείᾳ δυνάμει ἔν τισιν ἐπιδημεῖ ἢ πέμπει τὸν Χριστὸν αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὲρ τοῦ πιστεύοντας μὲν καὶ καταλαμβάνοντας αὐτοῦ τὴν θεότητα ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι πάσης κακοδαιμονίας, ἀπιστοῦντας δὲ μηδ᾿ ἀπολογίας ἔτι χώραν ἔχειν. ὡς παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἀκηκοέναι καὶ δεδιδάχθαι οὐ πιστεύσαντας. τίς οὖν λόγος παρίστησιν ἀκολουθεῖν ἡμῖν τὸ τὸν θεὸν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς εἶναι ὡς τοὺς νεοπλούτους τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδεικτιῶντας; οὐ γὰρ ἐπιδεικτιᾷ ὁ θεὸς πρὸς ἡμᾶς, βουλόμενος ἡμᾶς συνιέναι καὶ νοεῖν αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑπεροχήν· ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ γινώσκεσθαι ἡμῖν αὐτὸν ἐγγινομένην ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν μακαριότητα ἐμφύεσθαι ἡμῖν θέλων, πραγματεύεται διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀεὶ ἐπιδημίας τοῦ λόγου ἀναλαμβάνειν ἡμᾶς τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν οἰκείωσιν. οὐδεμίαν οὖν θνητὴν φιλοτιμίαν ὁ Χριστιανῶν λόγος καταμαρτυρεῖ τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: If you wish (θέλεις, singular, to Ambrose) us to meet (ἀπαντᾶν) even the most laughable things (καταγελαστότατα) of Celsus, hear him saying: 'But then, God being unknown (ἀγνοούμενος) among men and on account of this seeming (δοκῶν) to have less (ἔλαττον ἔχειν), would he wish (ἐθέλοι ἄν) to be known (γνωσθῆναι) and to make trial of (διαπειράσαι) both the believing and the unbelieving (πιστεύοντας, ἀπιστοῦντας), just like the newly rich (νεόπλουτοι) among men who are eager to show off (ἐπιδεικτιῶντες)? At any rate (γοῦν) they bear witness against (καταμαρτυροῦσι) God of a great and quite mortal (θνητήν) love of honour (φιλοτιμία).' We say then that God, being unknown by wicked (φαύλων) men, would wish to be known, not from his seeming to have less, but because knowledge (γνῶσις) of him releases (ἀπαλλάσσειν) the knower from unhappiness (κακοδαιμονία). But not wishing to test the believing or unbelieving does he either himself by unspeakable (ἀρρήτῳ) and divine power sojourn (ἐπιδημεῖ) in some, or send his Christ, but for the sake of the believing and grasping (καταλαμβάνοντας) his divinity (θεότης) being released from all unhappiness, and the unbelieving no longer having even room for a defence (ἀπολογίας χώραν), as not having believed through not having heard and been taught (ἀκηκοέναι, δεδιδάχθαι). What argument (λόγος) then establishes (παρίστησιν) that it follows (ἀκολουθεῖν) for us that God according to us is like the show-off newly rich? For God does not show off toward us, wishing us to understand and perceive (συνιέναι, νοεῖν) his pre-eminence (ὑπεροχή); but wishing to implant (ἐμφύεσθαι) in us the blessedness (μακαριότης) arising (ἐγγινομένην) in our souls from his being known by us, he works (πραγματεύεται) through Christ and the continual sojourn (ἀεὶ ἐπιδημία) of the Word for us to take up the kinship/familiarity toward him. So the Christians' teaching witnesses against God of no mortal love of honour.
pass_b_english: If you want us to answer even the most ridiculous of Celsus’s remarks, listen to what he says: “But then, would God, being unknown among men and thinking himself the worse off for it, wish to become known and to put to the test both those who believe and those who do not, like the newly rich among men who love to show off? They charge God with a great and altogether mortal love of honour.”

We say, then, that God, being unknown to wicked men, would wish to be known, not because he thinks himself the worse off, but because the knowledge of him frees the one who knows him from misery. Nor is it from a wish to test those who believe or those who do not that he either comes himself, by an ineffable and divine power, to dwell in certain people, or sends his Christ. He does it so that those who believe and grasp his divinity may be freed from all misery, while those who do not believe may no longer have room even for the plea that they did not believe because they had not heard and been taught.

What argument, then, shows that it follows from our teaching that God, as we conceive him, is like the newly rich among men who love to show off? For God does not show off before us out of a wish that we should understand and perceive his surpassing greatness. Rather, wishing to plant in us the blessedness that arises in our souls from our knowing him, he works through Christ and through the Word’s continual coming among us, so that we may take up our kinship with him. So the Christian teaching charges God with no mortal love of honour.

ὡς παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἀκηκοέναι clause recast as the plea unbelievers can no longer make ('no room even for the plea that they did not believe because they had not heard'); old 'as though' wording was ambiguous
'does not show off before us when he wishes us to understand' changed to 'out of a wish that we should understand': βουλόμενος gives the denied motive, contrasted with ἀλλὰ ... θέλων

Celsus fragment (from ἀλλὰ γὰρ to καταμαρτυροῦσι) put in quotation marks; its second sentence ('They charge God...') is read as Celsus speaking of the Christians, since Origen's closing sentence answers it word for word (θνητὴν φιλοτιμίαν ... καταμαρτυρεῖ). '(γοῦν)' is an editorial supplement in the staged text; rendered lightly ('They charge'). θέλεις is singular, addressed to Ambrose; rendered 'you'. φιλοτιμία rendered 'love of honour' (ambition for honour); κακοδαιμονία 'misery'. ἐπιδημία τοῦ λόγου rendered 'the Word's continual coming among us' (λόγος here the divine Word, so capitalised). οἰκείωσις rendered 'kinship' (close belonging). Possible but unclear allusion, not cited inline: unbelievers left without excuse (John 15:22; Romans 1:20). Review: βουλόμενος in οὐ γὰρ ἐπιδεικτιᾷ ... βουλόμενος is read as the motive Origen denies, set against the motive he affirms (ἀλλὰ ... θέλων); ὡς παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἀκηκοέναι ... οὐ πιστεύσαντας is read as the plea left to unbelievers.
